title: ISic020939. Graffito naming Hera

Apparatus criticus

  • Text after photograph

English translation

Valentina Mignosa

(To?) Hera

commentary

The complete name of Hera is scratched on the exterior of the rim of a fragmentary black-glaze patera. Scerra regards the graffito as one of the few secure pieces of evidence for cult practice at Kamarina and notes that no earlier evidence for the worship of Hera had been identified in the city. Comparable vase graffiti giving the complete name of the goddess are known from Gela. The vessel type was current from the last quarter of the fifth century through much of the fourth century BCE, but the absence of a secure archaeological context prevents a more precise dating. However, the orthography of the inscription—with open long /ɛː/ represented by epsilon and aspiration by het—would favour an earlier date, between the mid-sixth and early fifth century BCE. Scerra considers that the graffito could record a devotional act performed by a Geloan settler after the refoundation of Kamarina in 461 BCE, while also suggesting that the cult may have reached the city earlier. The inscription supports the presence of devotion to Hera but does not by itself demonstrate the existence of a formal sanctuary.
